summary: Describes an RTCP feedback message that reports per-packet arrival information such as loss, timing and ECN marks. Congestion control for RTP needs finer-grained feedback than the standard sender and receiver reports provide. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: To drive carefully, a sender needs to know which of its packages arrived and how fast. This document defines a detailed delivery receipt that the receiver sends back so the sender can adjust its speed.

subtitle: A standard RTCP report that tells an RTP sender which packets arrived, when, and with what ECN marks, so it can control congestion.

tldr.problem: Sender-based congestion control for interactive real-time media needs per-packet loss, timing and ECN information, which standard RTCP Sender and Receiver Reports do not give. Each algorithm had invented its own proprietary feedback message.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8888 defines an RTCP Transport-Layer Feedback Message (packet type 205, FMT 11) with a 16-bit metric for each RTP packet, giving received flag, ECN mark and arrival time offset, grouped by SSRC.
tldr.outcome: Different congestion control algorithms can share one feedback format. It is signaled in SDP with the ack parameter ccfb.

today: RFC 8888 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is meant to be used with RTP congestion control algorithms such as those in RFC 8698 and RFC 8298.

sections.title: Why Standard RTCP Reports Are Not Enough
sections.content:
Interactive real-time traffic such as video conferencing typically uses the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) over UDP. RTP offers no guarantee of reliability or timely delivery. The RTP Control Protocol (RTCP) lets a receiver send quality metrics back to the sender, and the sender can use them for congestion control.

Without a standard message, designers of congestion control algorithms built proprietary RTCP messages with only the parameters they needed, so the designs were not interoperable. This memo gives a common feedback format for unicast RTP that can be used by NADA (RFC 8698), SCReAM (RFC 8298), Google Congestion Control, and Shared Bottleneck Detection (RFC 8382), and hopefully by future algorithms.
sections.eli5: Every team used its own private way of reporting how the packages were doing. This document gives everybody one shared report form.

sections.title: What the Sender Needs to Know
sections.content:
From an analysis of those four algorithms, the RFC concludes that three pieces of information per RTP packet are needed:

  • RTP sequence number, so the sender can tell which packets were received and which were lost. Loss is a congestion signal for many algorithms.
  • Packet arrival time, because delay or delay variation (jitter) is a congestion signal for some algorithms.
  • ECN mark, the 2-bit mark showing not-ECT, ECT(0), ECT(1) or ECN-CE, when ECN is used on the path.

Reports are grouped by SSRC, one report block per received RTP stream. The RFC also warns that host OS interruptions can distort one-way delay estimates, so the sender should record send time at the last opportunity before transmitting and the receiver should record arrival time at the earliest opportunity.
sections.eli5: The sender wants three answers for every package: did it arrive, when did it arrive, and was the road marked as crowded?

sections.title: The Feedback Packet Format
sections.content:
The report is an RTCP Transport-Layer Feedback Message with packet type PT=205 and FMT=11. It can be sent in a regular scheduled RTCP report or as RTP/AVPF early feedback, and as early feedback it MAY be sent in a non-compound RTCP packet when the RTP/AVPF or RTP/SAVPF profile is used.

After the 8-octet RTCP header comes one report block per SSRC from which RTP packets have been received, and then a 32-bit Report Timestamp (RTS). Each block holds the SSRC, begin_seq, num_reports, and a 16-bit packet metric block for each sequence number in the range, calculated modulo 65536. If the count of metric blocks is odd, 16 bits of zero padding MUST be added. A block MUST NOT report more than 16384 packets, which is one quarter of the sequence space.

Each metric block has three fields:

  • R (1 bit): 1 if the packet was received. If 0, the other 15 bits are 0 and MUST be ignored.
  • ECN (2 bits): the echoed ECN mark, 00 if not received or ECN is unused.
  • ATO (13 bits): arrival time as an offset before the RTS, in units of 1/1024 second. An ATO of 512 means half a second before the RTS.

A value of 0x1FFE MUST be reported for an over-range measurement (more than 8189/1024 seconds), and 0x1FFF when the measurement is unavailable or the packet arrived after the RTS. The RTS is the middle 32 bits of an NTP format timestamp, from the same clock as the NTP timestamp in Sender Reports.
sections.eli5: The receipt lists every package number with a tick for arrived, a color for how crowded the road was, and how long ago it arrived, all measured back from the time the receipt was written.

sections.title: Reporting Rules and Frequency
sections.content:
Feedback packets SHOULD include a report block for every active SSRC. Consecutive reports are generally contiguous, but overlapping reports MAY be sent, which is needed when reordering crosses a report boundary. A packet reported as received MUST be reported as received in any later overlapping report, and later reports can update earlier data.

If duplicate copies of an RTP packet arrive, the arrival time of the first copy MUST be reported, and an ECN-CE mark MUST be reported if any copy was marked CE. If nothing arrived from an SSRC, a block MAY be sent with num_reports set to 0, or omitted. A loss report is not a request to retransmit.

If a feedback packet is too big for the path MTU, the sender SHOULD split it. There is a trade-off between speed, accuracy and overhead: feedback once per frame is often an upper bound, and some algorithms can work with an interval of 50-200 ms. Applications need to negotiate an appropriate interval at session setup.
sections.eli5: The receipt can list the same package twice if needed, and it always tells the truth about the first copy and about any crowded-road marks. Sending receipts too often costs more than it helps.

sections.title: When Feedback Packets Are Lost
sections.content:
RTCP packets have no sequence number, so a lost feedback packet has to be inferred from the time since the last one. Every RTP congestion control algorithm MUST specify how it reacts to lost feedback.

If a single feedback packet is lost, an appropriate response is to assume congestion stayed roughly the same. If several consecutive packets are lost, the media sender SHOULD rapidly reduce its sending rate, since this likely means a path failure. RFC 8083 on RTP circuit breakers gives further guidance.
sections.eli5: If one receipt goes missing, keep driving at the same speed. If many go missing in a row, slow down fast, because something is probably broken on the road.

sections.title: Signaling with SDP and ECN
sections.content:
A new ack parameter, ccfb, is defined for the a=rtcp-fb: SDP attribute. The payload type MUST be the wildcard type (an asterisk), so feedback covers all payload types, including FEC and retransmission. The example is a=rtcp-fb:* ack ccfb. If an offer lists several alternative congestion control feedback mechanisms, the answerer SHOULD pick only one.

The older RTCP ECN Feedback Packet of RFC 6679 duplicates the ECN information here. To use ECN, the offer MUST include a=ecn-capable-rtp: and ack ccfb, and MAY also include nack ecn. If both are offered, the answerer SHOULD signal one, not both. The RFC 6679 guidelines for starting, using and detecting failures of ECN MUST be followed, taking the information from the new packets.
sections.eli5: Before the call starts, both sides agree in the setup message that they will use this receipt form, and they pick only one kind of crowded-road report so nothing is sent twice.

sections.title: Design Rationale
sections.content:
SR and RR reports carry jitter, fractional loss and cumulative loss, but experience shows that is not enough for effective congestion control, which needs per-packet detail. The RFC compares alternatives:

  • TMMBR lets a receiver request a maximum bitrate. That is receiver-based, the opposite of the sender-based approach here, though it can complement it.
  • RTCP Extended Reports can be combined to carry loss, arrival time and ECN, but with high bandwidth and complexity overhead.
  • Transport-wide congestion control adds an RTP header extension with one sequence number across streams. It costs 8 octets per RTP packet and makes per-SSRC adaptation harder, so the RFC chose per-SSRC feedback.
sections.eli5: The old report was a summary, like a final score. Other fixes were either backwards, too heavy, or hid details, so the authors made a fresh per-package receipt.

sections.title: Security and Attacks
sections.content:
The security considerations of RTP, the RTP profile in use, and the congestion control algorithm apply. A receiver that sends inaccurate reports could trick the sender into sending faster than the path supports, causing congestion and possibly denial of service to other traffic. A sender can deliberately drop a packet, carefully, to check that the receiver reports the loss correctly.

An on-path attacker could alter reports to push the rate too high or too low. An off-path attacker would need to guess the SSRC and sequence number as well as the destination transport address. The secure RTCP profile in RFC 3711 can authenticate RTCP packets against both attacks.
sections.eli5: If someone lies on the receipt, the sender may drive too fast or too slow. Signing the receipts makes lying much harder.
